We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-4844)

The central question is whether instruction-tuned models develop attention heads that become structurally committed to the syntactic and positional regularities of their fine-tuning prompt templates — such that semantically equivalent inputs formatted differently produce systematically degraded or redistributed attention, not merely noisier outputs. The key concepts are: generalization surface collapse (the shrinking of the input distribution over which a model's learned behavior remains stable), sensitivity redistribution (perturbations that should be semantically neutral — paraphrase, reordering, delimiter substitution — instead cause disproportionate activation shifts in heads that had been reliably tracking instruction-relevant tokens), and attention pattern rigidity (the tendency for certain heads, particularly in early-to-mid layers, to lock onto template-specific positional anchors like \n\n, ###, or User: tokens rather than semantic content). An expert worries about something a beginner misses entirely: the failure mode is silent — the model still produces fluent, confident output, but the internal routing has degraded such that the "instruction-following" signal is now driven by spurious surface features rather than semantic intent, making the model brittle in exactly the deployment contexts (novel system prompts, API wrappers, multilingual templates) where robustness is most needed. Critically, this isn't a training data volume problem — it emerges specifically from the distributional narrowness of RLHF and supervised fine-tuning corpora, where a handful of prompt formats dominate, causing the model to treat template tokens as high-mutual-information anchors for task identity even when they carry no semantic content (Kung & Peng, 2023; Wang et al., 2023 on format sensitivity in instruction tuning; Zhou et al., 2023 on instruction-following robustness).

The mechanistic signature that separates template-anchor locking from normal positional encoding is position-invariant attention collapse: if a head is tracking a semantic role, scrambling the absolute position of a delimiter token (e.g., moving ### from position 4 to position 47) should degrade its attention weight on that token proportionally — but a rigidly template-locked head will follow the token, maintaining high attention regardless of absolute position, while a purely positional head will attend to the slot, not the content. Anthropic's attention head analysis in the sparse autoencoder work (Bricken et al., 2023) and Olsson et al.'s (2022) induction head circuits provide the baseline: induction heads show characteristic "stripe" patterns in attention matrices tied to token-identity repetition, not position per se — template-locked heads should show analogous stripes but conditioned on surface form of template tokens, detectable via activation patching when delimiter identity is held constant but position varies. The probing experiment design is: (1) construct a paired dataset of semantically identical instruction inputs across ≥5 template formats (ChatML, Alpaca, plain prose, Llama-2 system format, raw completion), (2) extract per-head attention weight vectors over the instruction token span, (3) train a linear probe on head activations to predict template identity independent of task identity — heads whose activations are decodable for template but not task are the rigidity-positive heads. A critical control is residual stream intervention: patch the residual stream at layer L from a correctly-formatted input into a misformatted one and measure task-accuracy recovery, isolating the layer-depth at which template surface features become load-bearing (Meng et al., 2022, ROME; Wang et al., 2022, IOI circuit). The numbers that would be diagnostic: if >30% of heads in layers 4–12 of a 32-layer model show template-decodability above 85% accuracy with a linear probe while task-decodability stays flat, that constitutes strong evidence of rigidity rather than incidental positional covariation. Existing work by Jain et al. (2023) on attention interpretability and Shi et al. The confound is real and was explicitly surfaced by Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2023) in their critique of activation patching: if later layers can compensate via residual stream superposition, patching layer L and observing output recovery conflates "layer L is sufficient" with "layer L plus downstream re-routing is sufficient," making causal claims unwarranted. The clean resolution is causal scrubbing with path-specific ablation (Chan et al., 2022): instead of patching a single layer's residual stream, you simultaneously freeze the direct path from the patched layer to the output logits while ablating all lateral connections from that layer to subsequent attention heads — this isolates whether the recovery signal travels through the hypothesized circuit path or leaks through alternative routes. Concretely, you'd run a three-condition experiment: (1) patch layer L residual stream only, (2) patch layer L and zero-ablate all Q/K/V projections in layers L+1 through L+4 that read from the patched positions, (3) patch layer L and noise-ablate (Gaussian, σ matched to activation variance) those same projections — if accuracy drops sharply from condition 1 to conditions 2/3, later-layer re-routing was load-bearing, not the patch itself. A second approach is logit lens attribution (Nostalgebraist, 2020; Belrose et al., 2023): project the residual stream at each layer directly onto the vocabulary and track when the correct task-relevant token probability exceeds chance — if the correct answer "locks in" at layer L in the patched run but not in the unpatched run, and stays locked through subsequent layers without further boosting, that supports layer L as causally sufficient rather than merely contributory. The numbers matter: in the IOI circuit (Wang et al., 2022), causal scrubbing recovered ~85% of the performance gap with <15% of the model's attention heads implicated, establishing that tight path-specific ablation can isolate genuine sufficiency — a template-rigidity experiment should target comparable specificity, and any recovery that requires >40% of downstream heads to remain intact should be treated as evidence of distributed re-routing rather than localized causal sufficiency. The irreducible epistemic limit is that in models using RoPE or ALiBi positional encodings, position information is re-injected at every attention layer, meaning no single-layer patch fully controls the positional signal — experiments on such models (LLaMA-2, Mistral) must additionally ablate the rotary components of Q/K projections at each layer to prevent positional re-anchoring from masquerading as content-based re-routing.

The key predictor of redistribution versus override is head utilization pressure measured by the effective rank of the value matrix output for the implicated heads: if a template-locked head's V-projection is already near full rank (utilizing most of its representational capacity for template-surface features), format-diverse fine-tuning has nowhere to write new semantic associations and will instead recruit additional heads in parallel — observable as an increase in attention entropy across the layer rather than a shift in the existing head's attention pattern (Dar et al., 2023 on weight space analysis of transformer heads; Michel et al., 2019 showing most heads are prunable precisely because they are low-rank and redundant). A second predictor is learning rate relative to head depth: shallow heads (layers 1–6 in a 32-layer model) that track positional anchors are updated with larger effective gradients during fine-tuning because they sit closer to the embedding layer where format signals are strongest — empirically, Chronopoulou et al. The distinction matters enormously for intervention design because redistribution and override have opposite failure modes under distribution shift: a redistributed head that now tracks semantic content will generalize to novel formats because its attention is driven by meaning, while an override architecture — a new head suppressing the old one — is fragile under any input perturbation that weakens the overriding head's signal, causing the original template-locked behavior to re-emerge, analogous to the "suppressor circuit" failure mode documented in Henighan et al. (2023) and the grokking-adjacent dynamics in Nanda et al. (2023) where circuits appear learned but are masked by stronger competing circuits. Practically, you can distinguish the two post-intervention outcomes by comparing attention weight correlation matrices before and after fine-tuning: redistribution produces a rotation of the existing head's attention pattern (high cosine similarity between old and new attention vectors across semantic-equivalent inputs), while override produces near-zero cosine similarity on the original head paired with emergence of a new high-entropy head at a different index. This matters because if your intervention produces override rather than redistribution, the correct follow-on action is surgical ablation of the template-locked head (setting its output weight matrix W_O to zero) combined with format-diverse fine-tuning, forcing the model to build semantic routing from scratch in that representational slot rather than papering over a brittle substrate — an approach consistent with the "head ablation then retrain" protocol implicit in Voita et al. (2019) on pruning redundant heads without accuracy loss.

A pretraining data intervention that would minimally reduce this is structural token randomization: replacing a random fraction (10–30%) of delimiter and markup tokens with semantically neutral alternates during pretraining, so no single surface form accumulates sufficient co-occurrence statistics to become a high-confidence positional anchor — this is a pretraining analog of the format-diverse fine-tuning discussed earlier, but applied before circuits consolidate, and is consistent with the data augmentation framing in Longpre et al. A more targeted objective-level intervention is span-level contrastive pretraining: for each document, generate a surface-permuted version (randomized delimiters, shuffled markup) and add a contrastive loss term penalizing divergence in intermediate layer representations between original and permuted versions — this directly pressures the model to build content-invariant representations at the layers where template locking occurs, analogous to the invariance objectives in Gao et al. (2021) SimCSE but applied during pretraining rather than fine-tuning. The hard constraint is induction head formation timing: Olsson et al. (2022) showed that induction heads form in a phase transition around 10^8–10^9 tokens and are foundational to in-context learning; any pretraining intervention that disrupts delimiter-tracking before this phase risks degrading the positional bootstrapping that induction heads rely on, meaning the intervention window is narrow — structural randomization should be applied after the induction head phase transition, requiring staged pretraining curricula that current open-source pipelines (LLaMA, Mistral) do not implement. The deepest implication is that minimizing template-locked circuit formation may be in fundamental tension with efficient in-context learning, since both rely on the same underlying mechanism of heads learning to track surface-form transitions as proxies for context boundaries — resolving this tension likely requires architectures that separate positional boundary detection from semantic content routing at the design level, rather than attempting to fix it through data or objective engineering alone.

A more implementable near-term modification is position-decoupled key normalization: normalize the key vectors in early-layer attention heads to remove the component aligned with the positional encoding direction before computing attention weights — this forces QK dot products to be driven by content rather than position-surface correlations, and is mechanistically cleaner than ALiBi or RoPE alternatives because it operates on the representation rather than the encoding scheme, preventing delimiter tokens from accumulating disproportionate key-norm mass (a known artifact documented in Xiao et al., 2023 where attention sinks form precisely because certain tokens develop anomalously large key norms). Explicit boundary tokens with isolated embedding tables — the most direct intervention — would assign delimiter tokens embeddings drawn from a separate parameter space that shares no dimensions with semantic token embeddings, implemented as a block-diagonal embedding matrix where boundary and content subspaces are orthogonal by construction; this prevents the model from ever representing "follows a delimiter" and "has semantic property X" in overlapping subspaces, and is consistent with the domain-token approach in Chronopoulou et al.
